summary: A snapshot of the protocol parameter assignments (numbers and keywords) used by the Internet protocol suite, such as protocol and port numbers. The live data was kept in online files, and this RFC reported on them. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 3232.

eli5.summary: A big phone book of numbers that tell computers which job each kind of message is for.

questions: what are well known port numbers
subtitle: A 1994 snapshot of the big registry of protocol numbers: IP protocol numbers, ports, ICMP types, ARP codes and much more.

tldr.problem: Internet protocols rely on many numbers and keywords (protocol numbers, port numbers, option codes) that must mean the same thing everywhere, so someone has to hand them out uniquely and write them down.
tldr.mechanism: The IANA keeps the assignments in a set of online text files. RFC 1700 is a snapshot made by pasting those files together with a minimum of formatting glue, covering dozens of registries from version numbers to terminal type names.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1700 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 3232, which points to the online database as the place to look instead of a printed snapshot.

today: RFC 1700 is Historic: it was obsoleted by RFC 3232. It obsoletes RFC 1340, and as a snapshot of online files it is no longer the place to look up current assignments.

sections.title: What This Snapshot Is
sections.content:
RFC 1700 is a status report on the parameters (numbers and keywords) used by protocols in the Internet community. It is a snapshot of an ongoing process: the assignments are kept up to date in a set of online text files, and the RFC was assembled by joining those files together with a minimum of formatting. The authors apologize for the rougher formatting and style than is typical of RFCs.

The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) is the central coordinator for assigning unique parameter values for Internet protocols. It is chartered by the Internet Society (ISOC) and the Federal Network Council (FNC), and is operated by the Information Sciences Institute (ISI) of the University of Southern California. Developers who need a link, socket, port or protocol number are told to contact the IANA.

The RFC says the common use of Internet protocols requires that the values in these fields be assigned uniquely. It replaces earlier editions, including RFC 1340 and RFC 1060, and it is itself marked Standards Track and listed as STD 2.
sections.eli5: When many people share one set of rules, everyone needs to agree on the numbers. One office, the IANA, hands out the numbers so that nobody gets the same one twice.

sections.title: Data Notations and Byte Order
sections.content:
The RFC states the conventions that every table in it relies on. Numbers are written in decimal, and data is pictured in big-endian order: fields are described left to right, with the most significant octet on the left and the least significant on the right.

The order of transmission is resolved to the octet level. When a diagram shows a group of octets, they are sent in the order they are numbered, which is the normal reading order in English. For a numeric value, the left-most bit in the diagram is the most significant bit, and bit 0 is the most significant. When a multi-octet quantity is sent, the most significant octet goes first.

The IEEE section later notes the opposite habit: the IEEE likes to write numbers in binary in bit transmission order, the reverse of the big-endian order used in Internet documentation.
sections.eli5: It is like agreeing to read a number from the left, biggest digit first. If everyone reads numbers the same way, nobody mixes them up.

sections.title: Special IP Addresses and Multicast Groups
sections.content:
The RFC says there are five classes of IP address, Class A through Class E. Classes A, B and C are used for unicast, Class D for multicast, and Class E is reserved for future use. With classless addressing (CIDR, described in RFC 1518 and RFC 1519), the network-number part of an address may be of any length and the classes matter less.

It then lists special cases written as {network, host} with -1 meaning all 1 bits. Examples: {0, 0} is this host on this network and may only be a source address; {-1, -1} is the limited broadcast, only a destination, and must never be forwarded outside the (sub)net of the source; {127, <any>} is the internal host loopback address and should never appear outside a host.

The multicast section, based on RFC 1112, lists group addresses. 224.0.0.1 is all systems on this subnet and 224.0.0.2 is all routers on this subnet. When used on an Ethernet or IEEE 802 network, the 23 low-order bits of the IP multicast address go into the low-order 23 bits of the multicast address 1.0.94.0.0.0.
sections.eli5: Some addresses are special, like the street name that means this house, or the one that shouts to everybody on the street. Multicast is a club address: only the computers that joined the club listen.

sections.title: Version Numbers and Protocol Numbers
sections.content:
The IP header has a 4-bit version field. The registry assigns 4 to the Internet Protocol (RFC 791) and lists other proposals of the time, such as ST, SIP, TP/IX, PIP and TUBA, in the slots from 5 to 9.

The 8-bit Protocol field in the IP header identifies the next-level protocol. A few well-known values are 1 ICMP, 2 IGMP, 4 IP in IP, 6 TCP and 17 UDP. Values 55 to 60 and 101 to 254 are listed as unassigned, and 0 and 255 are reserved. Most entries cite a defining RFC; some cite a person or an outside document, and the RFC notes that some of the items listed are undocumented.
sections.eli5: Every envelope has a small box that says what is inside: 6 means a TCP letter, 17 means a UDP postcard. The receiving computer reads the box and hands the letter to the right person.

sections.title: Well Known and Registered Ports
sections.content:
Ports name the ends of logical connections. For services offered to unknown callers, a service contact port is defined, sometimes called the well-known port. The same assignments are used with UDP where possible.

Well Known Ports are controlled by the IANA and on most systems can only be used by system (root) processes or privileged users. For many years they were in the range 0-255; the RFC says the IANA-managed range had recently been expanded to 0-1023. Registered Ports are not controlled by the IANA; on most systems ordinary user processes can use them. The IANA only registers or lists their use as a convenience, and they cover 1024-65535.

Entries include ftp 21, telnet 23, smtp 25, domain 53, bootps 67, bootpc 68 and tftp 69. Each is listed for both tcp and udp. Most of the RFC's length is made up of these two port tables.
sections.eli5: A building has one street address but many doors. Each door number is for a different service, like door 25 for mail. The low door numbers are the official ones, and the high ones are first come, first served.

sections.title: IP, ICMP and TCP Header Numbers
sections.content:
Several registries cover codes inside protocol headers. For IP options, options 0 and 1 are a single octet; every other option has a type octet, a length octet, and length-2 octets of data. The type octet splits into a 1-bit copied flag, a 2-bit class and a 5-bit option number. Examples: End of Options List (0), No Operation (1), Loose Source Route (131), Record Route (7).

The IP section also gives a recommended default time to live of 64 and a table of type-of-service values, such as 1000 for minimize delay and 0100 for maximize throughput. Only one TOS value can be requested in any one datagram. Recommended settings include minimize delay for TELNET and for FTP control, and maximize throughput for FTP data.

ICMP type numbers include 0 Echo Reply, 3 Destination Unreachable, 8 Echo and 11 Time Exceeded. TCP option kinds follow the same one-octet pattern for kinds 0 and 1, with entries such as 3 for Window Scale and 8 for the Time Stamp option.
sections.eli5: These are the little tick boxes and labels on the envelope: how urgent it is, what kind of note it is, and extra instructions. The registry says which number means which label.

sections.title: ARP, RARP and Ethernet Numbers
sections.content:
The ARP section lists operation codes: 1 REQUEST and 2 REPLY from RFC 826, 3 request Reverse and 4 reply Reverse from RFC 903 (RARP), then codes for DRARP and for the Inverse Address Resolution Protocol (RFC 1293). It also lists hardware types, such as 1 for Ethernet (10Mb) and 6 for IEEE 802 networks. The protocol type field reuses the Ethernet type codes.

The Ether Types section lists the type field values that tell what an Ethernet frame carries, including 0800 for Internet IP (IPv4), 0806 for ARP and 8035 for Reverse ARP. The RFC calls this list contributed, unverified information from various sources.

Other link-layer tables cover IEEE 802 SAP values, vendor prefixes of 48-bit Ethernet addresses (the first six hex digits match the vendor), Ethernet multicast addresses, X.25, MILNET, ProNET 80, XNS and PPP protocol field values.
sections.eli5: Before a computer can talk on a local wire it needs the number that says the message is an address question or an IP message. These tables hold those numbers, plus the code for the old trick where a machine asks, who am I?

sections.title: The Long Tail and What Replaced It
sections.content:
Beyond networking basics the RFC collects registries for DNS classes and types, Telnet options, mail keywords, BOOTP and DHCP parameters, MIME media types, character sets, SNMP management (the 1.3.6.1 branch of the OID name space) and private enterprise numbers under 1.3.6.1.4.1. It ends with lists of machine, operating system, terminal type and service names. Each registry cites the online file it came from.

The RFC itself says the live data is in the online files, so the printed copy is only a snapshot.
sections.eli5: The end of the book is a long list of odd little lists, like computer brand names. It is a copy of a list that keeps changing, so the book gets out of date.
